Learning Objectives
Learn how to obtain a thorough patient history and perform a complete physical examination
for patients with acute and chronic lateral ankle instability.
Develop an approach for the nonsurgical management of lateral ankle instability.
Identify patient factors that increase the risk for chronic lateral ankle instability.
Understand the association between hindfoot varus alignment and lateral ligament instability.
Understand surgical indications and techniques for the treatment of lateral ankle instability.
Overview/Pathophysiology
Most lateral ankle sprains occur when the ankle is in a position of plantar flexion and
inversion.

Acute lateral ankle instability is classified into three grades, depending on the severity of
ligament disruption.
With severe inversion, medial tibiotalar impingement may occur and result in pain or bone
bruising that is evident on MRI.
Epidemiology
Ankle sprains are one of the most common orthopedic injuries.
Ankle sprains may lead to chronic lateral ankle instability.

Epidemiology
Ankle sprains are among the most common injuries, with approximately 23,000
occurring each day in the United States.1,2 Approximately 15% to 25% of sports-related
injuries involve the lateral ankle ligament complex.3 Lateral ankle sprains account for
85% of all ankle sprains.3-6 Given the frequency at which these injuries occur, the
resultant loss in mobility and independence, and the need for recovery, substantial
disruption and costs are associated with disability and lost hours for amateur and
professional sports. Many terms are used to describe pathology of the lateral ankle
ligaments. Ankle sprains are an acute soft-tissue injury of the ankle. Laxity describes the
objective physical examination sign demonstrating an abnormal amount of motion
during assessment of the ligaments. Lateral ankle instability is symptomatic instability
resulting from pathology of the lateral ligaments over an acute or chronic timeline.
Chronic instability often is described by patients with recurrent ankle sprains.
As many as 10% to 30% of lateral ankle sprains may result in chronic lateral ankle
instability.7-11 Prognostic factors have been identified as possible predictors of poor
recovery. These factor include increasing age, amount of swelling, range of motion
restriction, presence of bone bruise, and athletes who may place greater loads/demands
on their ankles.12 Given the heterogeneity of the existing literature and specific factors
reported, no established tool can reliably determine a patient’s risk for poor recovery
after ankle sprain or the development of chronic instability.13

Anatomy and Biomechanics
Ligaments are composed mainly of type I collagen.
The ankle joint is afforded stability by its structure with the bony configuration of the ankle
mortise, including the distal tibia and fibula, and talar dome. The distal tibiofibular joint, known
as the syndesmosis, contributes to the stability of the lateral ankle.
The peroneal tendons are important dynamic stabilizers of the lateral ankle.
The lateral ankle complex consists of the anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL), the
calcaneofibular ligament (CFL), and the posterior talofibular ligament (PTFL).
The lateral talocalcaneal ligaments play a role in the stability of the lateral ankle.

Anatomy and Biomechanics
The ankle joint consists of the tibiotalar bony architecture and complex ligamentous and
soft-tissue supports. Normal ligaments are composed mainly of type I collagen, arranged
in parallel bundles that are in line with tensile stress. Ligaments have a proprioceptive
function thought to be mediated by mechanoreceptors and specialized nerve endings
that provide feedback to fine tune muscle balance and control. The lateral ligamentous
complex is a composite of three ligaments: the ATFL, CFL, and PTFL. A multiplanar
ligamentous complex is required to provide ankle stability in all positions during talar
and ankle mortise rotation and motion. The weakest of the three ligaments is the ATFL,
which is the most commonly injured. Occasionally, the ATFL is considered an
intraarticular thickening of the joint capsule. The ligament originates off the distal
anteroinferior fibula and inserts near the talar body and neck junction.14 The ATFL runs
parallel to the axis of motion in the flexion-extension plane with the ankle in neutral.15,16
In plantar flexion, the ATFL is under the most tension and, therefore, is the first and
most commonly injured ligament.17 The CFL originates from the distal fibula inferiorly
and travels beneath the peroneal tendons to insert onto the calcaneus at the lateral
tubercle. The CFL is involved in approximately 50% to 75% of injuries and rarely is
injured alone. The PTFL is injured in less than 10% of injuries likely because of its stout
resistance to failure in plantar flexion.3 The ligament exists as a capsular thickening
originating off the posterior fibula and inserting onto the lateral tubercle of the talus.
Substantial variability in the size, shape, and orientation of the lateral ligaments exists,
with as many as 75% of people having some variation.15 Most lateral ankle ligament

Pathology
The three phases of tendon healing are inflammatory, proliferative, and remodeling.
Ankle sprains typically are twisting injuries that occur during inversion of the foot while
supinated.
Associated injuries (peroneal tendon injuries, talar osteochondral lesions) are common.

Pathology
Lateral ligament injury most commonly occurs during anterolateral rotational motion.
This occurs if the foot is plantar flexed and supinated and the tibia rotates outwardly.
With increasing inversion of the foot, increased strain is placed on the lateral
ligamentous structures, resulting in the potential for ligament failure or strain. Most
commonly, with increasing degrees of plantar flexion, this mechanism predominantly
places force on the ATFL, which, therefore, is most commonly injured. At the time of
injury, an acute inflammatory cascade occurs. The cascade persists for 48 to 72 hours,
initiating the repair process and eventual healing. After the inflammatory phase is the
proliferative phase, during which fibroblast migration and the laying down of collagen
and protein occur. The remodeling phase occurs several weeks postinjury and is the
phase during which collagen maturation occurs. After injury, the predominant collagen is
type III.
The primary concern from a pathoanatomic perspective is that incomplete ligament
healing may predispose patients to recurrent injury, chronic instability, and possible
arthritis. Repetitive loading of injured ligaments results in improved collagen
proliferation and increased strength of healing tissue compared with those immobilized.

Risk Factors
Risk factors for lateral ligament instability include intrinsic and extrinsic factors.
Intrinsic factors include ligamentous laxity, cavovarus deformity, and prior injuries.
Extrinsic factors include athletic activities and contact trauma.

Risk Factors
Many risk factors may predispose a patient to lateral ligament injury. Globally, lateral
ankle instability may result from intrinsic and extrinsic factors. Although multiple
elements may contribute to a ligament injury, knowledge of a patient’s specific risk
factors may help define potential treatment options and their likelihood of success.
Intrinsic factors result from inherent biomechanical properties or patient-specific factors,
whereas extrinsic factors suggest an effect of an outside force. Intrinsic factors include
ligamentous laxity suggesting generalized hypermobility or abnormal soft-tissue
compliance affecting the inherent stability of the ankle, hindfoot cavovarus that
positions the foot in a mechanically disadvantageous position with additional stress on
the ATFL, and a history of prior trauma that may have altered the composition or
strength of the ligamentous tissues.18,19 In addition, a number of studies have evaluated
the role of bony or mechanical factors at the tibiotalar joint with regard to ankle stability.
Incongruency at the tibiotalar joint as a result of talar morphology, tibiotalar joint
alignment leading to reduced talar coverage, and/or altering loading profiles of the ankle
joint, as well as the position of the lateral malleolus may predispose patients to
instability.20-23 Mechanical factors also may aggravate existing instability. Anterior
osteophytes along the tibiotalar joint may limit dorsiflexion and, thereby, reduce stability
via loss of the inherent widening of the talus anteriorly. In addition, short gastrocnemius
muscles and contractures of the Achilles tendon complex may play a role in instability.
Alternatively, extrinsic factors include sporting events, particularly on uneven surfaces;
ball sports, such as soccer, rugby, and volleyball; and traumatic contact with another
player or his/her foot.24

Ankle instability typically is graded based on physical examination findings.
Functionally, the most important factor to determine is whether the injury is stable or
unstable.

Classification
Ankle sprains can be described simply as mild, moderate, or severe injuries. More
robustly, the grading of lateral ankle sprains is based on physical examination findings at
the time of injury. Two important terms require careful definition: mechanical and
functional instability. Functional instability describes the subjective sensation of
instability or giving out that a patient may report with activities. Mechanical instability
defines the objective laxity and anatomic abnormalities appreciated at the ankle,
typically in the ATFL and CFL. The historical grades increase in severity from grade I to
grade III; however, functionally, the most important aspect of these injuries is the
presence of a stable or unstable ankle. Grade I injuries are lateral ligamentous strains
without rupture of the ATFL with or without involvement of the CFL. Patients usually
have mild swelling and pain, with little to no restriction of active range of motion. No
laxity is noted on physical examination. Grade II injuries involve rupture of the ATFL with
an intact CFL. More swelling, range-of-motion restriction, and pain are present compared
with grade I injuries, with moderate functional disability. Grade III injuries are associated
with complete ruptures of the ATFL and CFL with or without PTFL involvement. More
considerable bruising and swelling generally are present, with an inability to bear weight.
True PTFL rupture is suspected to occur only in rare circumstances and generally in
patients with a high-grade injury and associated ankle dislocation injury patterns.
Overall, the key differentiator is between grade II (stable) and grade III (unstable) injuries;
however, distinguishing these injuries may be difficult in the acute setting.3 The recovery
period is longer for grade II and grade III injuries, with studies reporting that return to
full activity may take 6 or more weeks; however, residual functional limitations may be
present for as long as 1 year postinjury13 (Table 1).

Evaluation/Diagnosis
Evaluation
A thorough patient history and physical examination, with appropriate diagnostic tests and a
high index of suspicion, guide the physician through an effective evaluation.
The Ottawa Ankle Rules can be used to determine if radiographs are indicated.
Advanced imaging studies are required in a small subset of patients.
Ankle instability results from a complex interplay of anatomic, biomechanical, and functional
pathology, which presents difficulty in assessing the underlying causes. A paucity of
evidence-based, standardized tests are used in the diagnosis of ankle instability.25
Patient History
Determine the mechanism of injury, typically an inversion mechanism.
A focused patient history to elicit intrinsic and extrinsic risk factors is useful to target potential
etiologies.
Ability to bear weight postinjury may help determine injury severity and associated injuries.

Patient History
Lateral ankle ligament injuries typically occur with an inversion mechanism of injury.26-28
Patients report the ankle giving way or rolling. They also may describe feeling or hearing

regarding the need for additional imaging studies according to the Ottawa Ankle Rules;
however, little data links the reported injury history with severity or diagnosis of injury.
Overall, the patient history should focus on risk factors associated with potential
underlying mechanical causes for instability or recurrent instability. A careful directed
patient history evaluating intrinsic factors that may contribute to risk for lateral ligament
injury should be documented. A brief review of extrinsic factors that may have
contributed to the acute episode of instability also should be detailed.
Physical Examination
Pain and swelling may limit the initial physical examination.
Careful palpation of all potentially injured structures is imperative.
Special tests used to assess the lateral ligaments include the anterior drawer and talar tilt tests
(Figure 1).
Initial, day-of-injury assessment of the patient is a triage mechanism to rule out fracture and
associated injuries. Initial physical examination does not provide adequate clarity to guide
diagnosis or evaluation of the injury grade.29
Delayed assessment (4 to 8 days postinjury) allows for a more accurate and detailed
evaluation.29

Physical Examination
Some aspects of the physical examination may be limited at the time of initial
presentation because of pain and swelling. Therefore, a repeat physical examination is
recommended approximately 4 to 7 days postinjury. A physical examination completed 5
days after the initial examination has a specificity of 84% and a sensitivity of 96% in
determining if a lateral ligament rupture is present.15 Localized tenderness, swelling,
and ecchymosis over the ATFL and/or the CFL is consistent with acute lateral ligament
injury. Focal or localized pain in a patient with bruising along the lateral ankle is
associated with a 90% likelihood of lateral ligament injury.29 The physical examination

should include a detailed examination of potentially concurrent injured structures,
including the medial and lateral malleoli, base of the fifth metatarsal, midfoot, deltoid
ligament complex, syndesmosis, tibiotalar joint, peroneal tendons, and proximal fibula. A
patient who is unable to bear weight may indicate other associated diagnoses, such as
an osteochondral injury or associated fracture.30
Special tests for assessment of acute lateral ankle instability include the anterior drawer
and talar tilt tests. These tests cannot be reliably performed in the acute setting because
of pain and swelling.29,31 The talar tilt test evaluates CFL ligamentous integrity. A firm
endpoint indicates a stable ankle, and increased laxity indicates CFL ligament injury. The
test is performed by placing stress on the lateral ankle to evaluate stability.32 The
anterior drawer test requires application of anteriorly directed force on the ankle/talus
while the tibia is stabilized, thereby evaluating the ATFL.33 The anterior drawer test may
demonstrate anterior talar subluxation or a sulcus sign. A plantar flexed position during
the anterior drawer test isolates the ATFL, whereas neutral plantar flexion tests the CFL.
Comparison of these tests to the (uninjured) contralateral limb is important to establish
a baseline if possible. Physical examination findings of focal tenderness and bruising on
the lateral ankle combined with an anterior drawer test are associated with a 98%
sensitivity and 84% specificity for the diagnosis of an ATFL tear.29,31 All patients with
acute ligamentous ankle instability or recurrent instability should be assessed for
cavovarus hindfoot anatomy. Surgeon should assess for hindfoot varus alignment, a
peek-a-boo heel, and an elevated or exaggerated medial foot arch (Figure 2). A Coleman
block test and assessment of gastrocsoleus tightness may better elucidate mechanical
causes of lateral ankle instability.

Neurovascular Examination
With any extremity injury, a complete neurovascular examination of the affected limb is
imperative. In addition to ligamentous injuries, traction injuries of the superficial
peroneal or sural nerves may occur in combination with inversion ankle injuries.
Although vascular injuries in combination with closed ankle inversion injuries are rare,
establishing normal perfusion of the affected extremity is important.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
The Ottawa Ankle Rules can help determine if radiographs are indicated.
AP, lateral, and mortise radiographs should be obtained with the patient bearing weight if
possible.
Stress radiographs are not routinely used in the assessment of acute lateral ankle instability.
Positive anterior drawer test: stress radiographs demonstrate 3 mm greater translation
compared with the opposite side or an absolute value of 10 mm

Radiography
The Ottawa Ankle Rules outline indications for radiographic investigation in patients with
an ankle injury. This determination requires examination of the medial and lateral
malleoli for bony tenderness to palpation and assessment of weight-bearing status at
the time of injury. Bony tenderness of the distal 6 cm of each malleolus, base of the fifth
metatarsal, or navicular indicate the need for radiographs. Inability to bear weight at the
time of injury or inability to take four steps at the time of physical examination also
meets the criteria for radiographs. Following these rules may reduce unnecessary
radiographs in patients with uncomplicated ankle sprains. The Ottawa Ankle Rules are
associated with a 99% sensitivity for the detection of fractures if performed within 48
hours postinjury.30

If radiographs are indicated, standard views of the ankle should be obtained with the
patient bearing weight if possible. These include AP, mortise, and lateral views. If
tenderness exists about the anterior calcaneus, midfoot, or fifth metatarsal, then weight-
bearing views of the foot also should be obtained.
Stress radiographs are not routinely indicated in the assessment of acute lateral
instability because they are unreliable for prognostication and are operator
dependent.34-38 Stress radiographs can be performed with varus talar tilt on the AP
view, with assessment of the degree of talar tilt being measured. More than 3° of tilt
compared with the contralateral side or more than 10° of tilt overall is considered
abnormal. Lateral stress views obtained while performing an anterior drawer test also
have been described, with a 3-mm difference compared with the contralateral side or an
absolute value of 10 mm considered abnormal34 (Figure 3).

setting.

MRI is most useful in investigating other pathology (peroneal tear, occult fractures,
osteochondral lesions of the talus, bone bruising, tarsal coalition, or impingement lesions).
MRI should be considered if pain persists for 8 weeks following ankle sprain.

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI can provide excellent detail, allowing for identification of osteochondral lesions of
the talus, injury to the lateral ligaments or the deltoid ligament complex, injury the distal
syndesmosis, and the integrity of the peroneal tendons. A 3T magnet MRI affords better
image clarity than a regular MRI and, with experience, may allow for assessment of injury
grade.18 MRI is a useful imaging modality if concern for injury to additional structures
(beyond the lateral ankle ligaments) exists or if recovery is not progressing as expected.
Studies have suggested that MRI may be useful to guide the treatment of elite athletes
and provide potential prediction of outcome.39,40
Ultrasonography
Ultrasonography is a useful imaging modality to detect acute ATFL injuries (Figure 4).
Additional studies are necessary to elucidate the role of this imaging modality in diagnosis and
prognosis.

Ultrasonography
Ultrasonography may be a useful imaging modality for the evaluation of the
musculoskeletal system. The use of ultrasonography for the evaluation of ankle
instability shows promise. In one study, ultrasonography accurately detected ATFL tears
in 91% of patients compared with 97% for MRI. Despite this finding, robust studies on
the use of ultrasonography in patients with ankle instability are limited, and it is not
recommended as the preferred diagnostic imaging modality.41,42 Finally,

Management
Nonsurgical Management
Initial acute management for all grades of injury consists of rest, ice, compression, and
elevation (RICE)
A semirigid brace during functional activities facilitates recovery better than limiting–weight
bearing or immobilization.
Functional instability should be managed via a course of physical therapy emphasizing
isometric exercises and resistance training, peroneal strengthening, range of motion, and
proprioceptive training.
Maximizing the resistive function of the peroneal musculature may offset mechanical
ligamentous instability.

Nonsurgical Management
Many systematic reviews of the literature have examined the effectiveness of various
treatment protocols for the management of lateral ankle sprains. Consensus exists that
early management should consist of RICE. This protocol allows for the natural stages of
healing for ligamentous tissue.43 During the inflammatory phrase of healing, the goals of
management include swelling control and prevention of additional injury. RICE therapy
provides acute control of pain and swelling to minimize early symptoms.44 Cryotherapy
is most effective in the first 3 to 5 days postinjury.45 Controversy exists with regard to
the utility of immobilization in the acute setting. Evidence for early mobilization and early
short-term immobilization exist, resulting in some ambiguity with regard to the optimal
approach;46,47 however, longer term immobilization generally is considered detrimental
in these acute injuries.48 Higher grade injuries likely benefit from a short period (10 days

18/43

or fewer) of immobilization. The Collaborative Ankle Support (CAST) trial demonstrated
improved early mobilization and overall recovery in these patients.47
As recovery continues and patients move into the proliferative phase of ligamentous
recovery, protected, controlled stress on the tissues should be encouraged. Functional
rehabilitation promotes healing of the collagen fibers into their native orientation, which
reduces the risk of weaker, disorganized type III collagen deposition.49 Protective
functional recovery should involve the use of tape or a semirigid brace to enhance
symptom relief and joint stability while promoting mobilization. The use of a rigid form
of ankle support appears beneficial with regard to the timing of return to work and sport
and substantially improves symptoms compared with an elastic bandage or prolonged
immobilization.47,48 Therefore, a combined protective ankle support and an early
functional rehabilitation treatment program are strongly advocated and supported.46,50
Weight-bearing restrictions should not be instituted for lateral ankle sprains because
early weight bearing and functional rehabilitation result in faster recovery and greater
patient satisfaction.
Additional adjuvants for nonsurgical management include NSAIDs and cortisone
injections. NSAIDs have been well studied and supported by the literature for symptom
control in the acute phase of ankle sprains.51,52 Although NSAIDs may be useful for pain
control in the initial recovery phase in patients with no medical contraindications for
their use, cortisone injections should not be used in the acute setting. Cortisone has a
negative effect on ligament healing in the acute injury setting because it adversely
affects the inflammatory cascade and fibroblast function and, thereby, inhibits collagen
synthesis. No evidence supports the use of platelet-rich plasma or prolotherapy in the
management of acute ankle ligament injuries.53 Electrical stimulation and therapeutic
ultrasonography as adjuvant modalities for the management of ankle sprains are not
supported in the current literature.54
After the acute management of acute instability, patients may continue to experience
residual functional instability. Functional instability should be managed via a course of

Most ankle sprain injuries are successfully managed nonsurgically, and surgical
management offers no improvement in outcome;55 however, in select patients, such as
those with recurrent instability or professional athletes, surgical repair may be indicated.
In the acute setting, a Cochrane review failed to demonstrate any advantage of acute
surgical management over nonsurgical management. In fact, the study reported a
seemingly higher rate of complications, longer recovery, increased stiffness, and surgical
complications in the surgical group compared with the nonsurgical cohorts.56 Despite
this finding, objective measures of mechanical instability on physical examination via
anterior drawer testing and radiographic stress testing are substantially less common

indicated in professional high-level athletes, particularly given that Verhagan et al57
reported objective residual ankle instability was a predictor of future ligamentous ankle
injury.58 Overall, most patients should be treated nonsurgically given the high rates of
success.

ligaments are directly repaired with the use of suture, bone tunnels, and/or suture
anchors. Patients are immobilized for 2 weeks postoperatively, after which an early

12 weeks postoperatively.

complications and accelerate recovery. The arthroscopic technique is technically
challenging and dependent on a good-quality remnant ligament. No biomechanical
difference has been reported with regard to the strength of the arthroscopic and

those reported for open, direct repair. Widespread adoption of this technique may be
limited by a steep learning curve.
Anatomic reconstruction with graft is indicated in patients with poor-quality native tissue
or limited ligament remnants. This is more likely after a long period of instability. Other
indications for anatomic reconstruction with graft include high body mass index, failed
previous lateral ligament repair, and generalized ligamentous laxity.
Free autograft options include semitendinosus, gracilis, plantaris, Achilles tendon, and
palmaris longus. Local graft options include the peroneus brevis tendon and the
extensor digitorum longus. Autografts are beneficial for superior tissue quality; however,
donor site morbidity is the primary disadvantage.
Allograft options include tensor fascia latae, tibialis anterior, and those listed for free
autografts. Allograft can be used in patients with poor quality native tissue. The
advantages of allograft are the shorter surgical time and no donor site morbidity.
Allografts are associated with a very low risk of disease transmission, heal more slowly,
and are costly.
